reading.body:
Profit Finder Pro Software is not a data center and should not be counted in any assessment of AI infrastructure or grid capacity in Arizona.

The listing is a customer relationship management and sales-tracking product sold to small businesses in roofing, solar, contracting, and insurance. Its address in Maricopa County, Arizona sits in the Scottsdale area, and the specific suite is currently occupied by a different company, TraVek Inc. Nothing publicly available connects the software business or the address to server infrastructure, colocation space, or dedicated data center equipment.

The entry originates as a mistagged OpenStreetMap point labeled telecom=data_center. No capacity figure is published for it, and the record carries zero megawatts. It sits several miles from the other eight rows in its batch, so no shared building links them. The pattern is a scattered set of independently mistagged small businesses across the Phoenix metro rather than a cluster around one site.

For AI specifically, the consequence is arithmetic. This row contributes nothing to the 512 MW of published capacity mapped across Arizona's four facilities with published figures. Mistags like this one inflate facility counts without adding load, which matters because the grid constraint on AI scaling is measured in megawatts and interconnect queues, not in address points. A reader counting data centers from a raw map extract would overcount Arizona sites while the power total stayed the same.

What the data does not cover is whether any real data center exists at these coordinates under another name, or how many similar mistags remain in the wider dataset. It establishes only that this one listing, on the sources checked, is a software office and not a building that draws power.
